title: The Long Road | Buddhism: What Makes You Not a Buddhist
subtitle: All compounded things are impermanent; all tainted phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are without self; nirvana is peace.
body:
## Preface

By chance, I came across this book. Its author is Dzongsar Jamyang Khyentse Rinpoche, one of the teachers of Tibetan Buddhism.
Unlike Buddhist books that begin with karmic wrongdoing, reincarnation, and accumulating merit, this book explains Buddhism’s most profound, central views.
“Clarifying the essentials of impermanence, emptiness, and liberation; guiding sentient beings away from the hardships of life, to look back at themselves, explore their original mind, attain realization, and strengthen their confidence in life.”
This is not a book explaining Buddhist concepts or customs. The author makes clear in the preface that it will not discuss techniques of sitting meditation, practices, or mantras. Instead, it explains Buddhism’s core ideas, the “Four Views” (Four truths), from various perspectives on life.

> All compounded things are impermanent; all tainted phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are without self; nirvana is peace.

## All Compounded Things Are Impermanent
Translated, this means “Everything that is put together is impermanent.” Nothing consists of a single constituent, and nothing is eternal. Here, “the concept of impermanence is neither a prophecy of the end of the world or apocalypse, nor a punishment for human sin.” From my own perspective: even though present-day science has separated matter down to the level of quarks, we cannot guarantee that quarks have no constituents. That things are not eternally unchanging is an eminently reasonable view. We study conservation of momentum, and conservation of energy. If we continue, we also study conservation of parity and CPT. But none of this is the end. As these theories develop and become more complete, as humans continually broaden the boundaries of knowledge, we also continually revise our previous conservation laws—our unchanging truths. I find it hard to imagine a day when humanity can discover that “first truth of the universe.” The world as I understand it is always changing. Although physics has always sought “invariance amid myriad changes,” this invariance is itself continually revised. That process of revision can be understood as “impermanence.”

## All Tainted Phenomena Are Suffering
The Tibetan term here is *zagbcas*. The translator renders it as “taints,” and also as “emotions” in the book. In Chökyi Nyima Rinpoche’s *Indestructible Truth*, *zagbcas* is explained as “related to falling or shifting.” It can be understood as: all that decays is suffering. Humans pursue emotions. Most pursue happiness. Whether it is the thrill of playing games, the satisfaction of eating, or the joy of reading, its essence is a feeling of happiness. But a smaller number pursue pain. Among them are artists who firmly believe “art comes from suffering,” Puritans who believe “we are born in original sin and must spend our lives atoning,” and even masochists who simply enjoy being hurt. (With the last group, I find it hard to distinguish whether they like pleasure or pain, or both.) Yet these emotions and desires themselves are suffering. Sometimes these desires seem to bring us temporary happiness. But if you can step outside and observe, you will find that “desire is learned.” Often, we want something—luxurious possessions, the respect of others, an exalted position—because life in the secular world continually teaches us to pursue it, not because we need it. In the era of the commodity economy, this teaching is even dressed up in more high-sounding terms: “Great companies don’t investigate users’ needs; they create needs.” We delight in saying this, as though such companies are tremendously impressive, as though they are leading the trends of the age. Yet sometimes we forget to ask whether those needs themselves are necessary. I am not opposed to technology, nor have I ever thought an age without technology was better. Science and technology are tools. But those of us who use them sometimes lack an original mind of self-awareness, carrying countless desires as we use technology to develop still more desires.

## All Phenomena Are Without Self
Attachment to the self is the root of all suffering and disappointment. Leung Man-tao wrote a book titled *Attachment to Self* (我执). In his explanation of the title, he writes: “I know it all now: all these lies and delusions, baseness and cowardice. Like pigments and materials, they are just enough to paint an entire city, with its countless scenes and encounters. What you see is merely your own imagination; what you think is yours is merely a coincidence. The tighter you grasp, the more futile it becomes. This is attachment to self.”

First comes “self,” then “attachment.” We are always affirming the self, always doing our utmost to prove its existence. Sometimes this proof becomes things we buy: satisfying “self-identification” through “a sense of ownership of things.” Sometimes it becomes stubbornness, reinforcing the illusion of “I am myself” through the uniformity of emotion or behavior. The things you buy are not yours; you only possess them temporarily. More deeply, even possession is too much to say: you only temporarily “think you possess them.” Then there is all that infatuation in relationships: “How laughable the world of dust, how tedious infatuation; better to hold everything in disdain.” Too many joys and sorrows, partings and reunions, are also essentially the mistaken belief that the other person is a part of oneself. Your partner is not your possession; they are another independent individual and do not belong to you.

## Nirvana Is Peace
I am slow-witted. I have not yet grasped this one, and dare not presume to speak of understanding it.

## Afterword
One final small thing I gained from reading this book: Siddhartha taught sentient beings using different explanations according to each person’s life experience and way of understanding. That is why there are so many Buddhist schools and so many precepts that are not entirely the same. I even think the “hells” and “karmic obstacles” discussed in Buddhism were also Siddhartha’s way of tailoring his teaching to individuals. The source still lies in these Four Views. If one can see through these four points, the detailed concepts of hells and karmic obstacles can also be set aside. The path itself is not the point, much less the destination.
